# Job arrays {#sec-arrays}

::: {.tldr}
A job array runs the *same script* many times, each with a different index
(`$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID`). One `sbatch`, one script, N independent tasks the scheduler spreads
across the cluster and backfills into gaps. MedicineBow allows arrays up to **10,000** tasks.
:::

## The problem it solves

You have 500 parameter combinations to sweep, or 500 raster tiles / watersheds / weather-days
to process. A bash loop runs them serially in one job, so one crash near the end wastes
everything. Copy-pasting 500 submit scripts is no better. An **array job** is one script,
submitted once, that Slurm turns into 500 independent tasks it can run in parallel and
backfill wherever there's room.

## The mechanics

Add `--array` and use `$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` to pick which piece of work this task does:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
#SBATCH --job-name=sweep
#SBATCH --array=1-500                 # 500 tasks, indices 1..500
#SBATCH --qos=fast                    # short independent tasks → high-priority QOS
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00               # per task
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=logs/sweep-%A_%a.out # %A = array job id, %a = task index

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 python/3.12.0

# Use the task index to select this task's work:
python run_case.py --case-id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
```

Submit once:

```bash
mkdir -p logs
sbatch submit_array.sh        # creates 500 tasks: 12345_1, 12345_2, ... 12345_500
```

Each task is scheduled independently. Because they're small and short, they backfill well
(@sec-priority) and the whole sweep finishes faster than running them in series.

## Driving work from the index

The index is just a number; you map it to real work. Common patterns:

**Line N of a parameter file:**

```bash
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" params.txt)
python run.py $PARAM
```

**The Nth input file:**

```bash
FILES=(/project/cowy-firesurro/data/tiles/*.tif)
THIS=${FILES[$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID]}      # note: arrays are 0-indexed in bash
python process.py "$THIS"
```

(If you index files from a bash array, start `--array=0`; if you use `sed -n Np`, start
`--array=1`. Off-by-one here is the classic array bug.)

## Throttling

Cap how many tasks run simultaneously with `%`:

```bash
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20        # at most 20 tasks running at a time
```

This keeps you under your account's core cap (and protects your fair-share, @sec-priority)
while still processing all 500. A modest `%` limit is often faster overall, because you stop
competing with yourself and stay backfill-friendly.

## Managing an array

```bash
squeue --me                     # shows pending tasks collapsed, e.g. 12345_[6-500]
scancel 12345                   # cancel the whole array
scancel 12345_7                 # cancel just task 7
sacct -j 12345                  # per-task outcomes after the fact
```

To find which tasks failed (so you can rerun only those):

```bash
sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,State,ExitCode -n | grep -v COMPLETED
```

then resubmit just those indices: `sbatch --array=17,43,88 submit_array.sh`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Arrays vs. MPI jobs
An array is for **independent** tasks that don't communicate: sweeps, ensembles, per-file
pipelines. If your tasks must talk to each other — a single domain-decomposed simulation — use
an **MPI** job instead (@sec-ladder).
:::

Arrays are also the natural unit for **ensembles** — fire-weather members, hydrologic
scenarios, Monte-Carlo draws — one array task per member, each writing to its own output,
collected afterward.
